oneLine: A full blackjack table for up to three seats sharing one screen: every bet a real table books, every rule that changes what the game costs, six side bets with computed paytables, and a strategy trainer and card counter that tell you what the felt never will.
status: Feature complete, measured, and through eight rounds of adversarial review. Everything is green: 183 unit tests, typecheck, lint with zero errors and zero warnings, a production build, and the full statistical suite. The engine went through an optimisation pass (66x faster per round) and two correctness passes. Round one of judging found four rule defects; round two confirmed those fixed and found five more, including a money bug in the persist path and a house-edge model that told the player they held an advantage; round three confirmed those and found three more, including a crash when the shoe ran dry mid-round; round four found a persisted shape that no longer loaded, a counter that lost the felt across a mid-round reshuffle, and three tests and documents that claimed more than they checked; round five found a wrong basic-strategy cell at the default table, a graded decision the store threw away, a rules change that could leave a wager the bankroll could not cover, a dealer reference table that was itself wrong, and a house edge measured against the wrong denominator; round six confirmed all ten fixed and found that the counting trainer was calibrated for Hi-Lo alone (Knock-Out read a 10.4% player disadvantage off an untouched shoe), that the denominator fix had reached the simulation and not the stats panel a player actually reads, that the global key handler swallowed Enter and Space from every focused button, and that side-bet edges were printed for six decks at every deck count; round seven confirmed all ten fixed, settled the Vegas Strip question as noise (pooled over three million rounds: 0.408% +/- 0.066 against a model of 0.400%), and found thirteen more — among them a Lucky Ladies figure the code called exact while its own comment called it an approximation, two round-six fixes that shipped with no test at all, a session statistic that excluded naturals which pushed, and a README row printing a single-seed point estimate beside three exact ones. round eight confirmed six of eight fixes effective and found two that were not: the early-surrender cells were applied before the few-deck and no-hole-card patches and silently overwritten by both, producing a chart that surrendered hard sixteen against an ace while hitting eight-eight against an ace; and the autoplay bet ramp, index plays and even-money branch were all wired to a bot config `setBot` could set and nothing in the app called. Both are fixed — the chart patch order reversed with a test over the whole rule cross-product, and the two bot switches surfaced in the counting panel. All are fixed, each with the test that would have caught it.

whatWasBuilt.summary: Built from nothing in one session, in the shape the craps table next door established: a pure engine, a store that is only a metronome, and a felt that is an SVG print with HTML on top of it. The engine came first and was driven by tests, which found six genuine bugs before any UI existed.
engine: types.ts — cards, hands, seats, rules, records. Money is integer cents everywhere; see money.ts for why.
rng.ts — xoshiro128** with rejection sampling. An honest copy of the craps one rather than a shared package across two apps that never deploy together.
shoe.ts — a fixed array plus a pointer, not a shifted queue. The cut card sits at a fraction of the shoe.
hand.ts — totals, soft/hard, and every legality question, each returning a reason rather than a boolean.
rules.ts — five presets and the published per-rule edge deltas the setup screen prices switches with.
sidebets.ts — six paytables with edges computed by enumeration, not looked up.
table.ts — the state machine. Every legal move, returning a new table or a refusal with a sentence in it.
resolve.ts — settlement. The only function that pays anybody.
strategy/basic.ts — the chart, per rule set, with the table's own restrictions folded into the cells.
strategy/counting.ts — Hi-Lo, KO, Omega II, Hi-Opt II, the Illustrious 18 and the Fab 4.
strategy/autoplay.ts — the bot, which moves money only through the same exported actions the buttons call.
ui: An SVG felt at a fixed 1000x560 viewBox with HTML positioned in the same coordinate space, scaled by one transform.
Cards are the shared 54-PNG deck from cardArt/, copied into public/cards, with a CSS 3D flip and a CSS-drawn back.
Chips are drawn in CSS — a conic gradient makes the eight rim dashes without eight elements.
Fifteen synthesised sounds, no audio assets: cards, chips, the sweep, the shuffle, and three stings that decide money.
A stats panel that is beside the felt above 1180px and a drawer below it.
bugsFoundByTests: advance() moved the focus after every action, so a hit that did not bust passed the turn to the next hand.

An early surrender that finished the last hand set the phase to DEALER and skipped the peek entirely — which under ENHC meant the dealer never drew a second card, and with a live Bust It bet meant it never resolved.
closeOffers() could land on PLAYER with a null focus when every hand was a natural, hanging the round forever.
settle() had no idempotence guard, so a double-fired phase transition paid the table twice.

The split-to-four limit was reported with the wrong reason because the test fixture ran out of pairs — the engine was right and the test was wrong, which is worth recording because it looked like the opposite.
Two zustand selectors (advice(), count()) built a fresh object on every store read, which is an infinite render loop. Found by running the app, not by a test; they are hooks now.
setBet() enforced the side-bet cap in one direction only, so lowering the wager left a side bet above it. Found by hand-tracing.

bugsFoundByReview.summary: A judging pass against the craps table's standard found four rule defects that 118 passing tests did not. Each is now fixed with the test that would have caught it — and the pattern in all four is the same: the tests asserted that a rule *refused* correctly and never that it *worked*.
defects: Re-split aces was a dead switch. split() marked both hands finished the moment their card landed, so a third ace could never be split — while the setup screen priced the rule at 0.08%, ruleEffects() printed it, the README advertised it, and the liberal preset shipped it on. The only RSA test exercised the refusal branch. No house-edge measurement at any feasible sample size would have caught it; the test that does is splits-per-thousand with the rule on versus off.

Even money paid the wrong amount at 6:5. It is implemented as insurance for the maximum, which is exactly 1:1 only when the payout is 3:2 — the identity needs x = 1/2 from the dealer-natural branch and x = p - 1 from the other, and those agree at no other p. On a $10 bet at the single-deck preset it returned $10 or $7 depending on the hole card. The offer is now refused anywhere but 3:2, with insurance still available.
Even money was accepted against a dealer ten. It never checked the upcard, and early surrender opens the offers phase on a ten.

Lucky Ladies' 1000:1 line was lost to a split. Settlement recomputed the jackpot from hands[0].cards, which after a split holds one queen and whatever was drawn to it. The upgrade is now recorded on the wager at grade time (SideBetWager.jackpot) while the cards it was graded on are still the hand.
alsoFixed: The basic-strategy chart had no ENHC variant, and holeCard was missing from the chart cache key — so a no-hole-card table was served a peeking chart, and whichever was requested first was served to both.
The single- and double-deck chart deltas were applied as one set at both deck counts, contradicting the comment above them. They are two sets now.

playRound folded insurance and side-bet results into net while leaving their stakes out of wagered, so the counting comparison measured an edge against the wrong denominator. Per-bet figures now come out of the settlement list, which already says which bet each movement belongs to.
betRamp existed twice — once in counting.ts for the HUD and once in autoplay.ts for the bot — so the panel could advise one bet while the bot placed another.
The persist merge refunded unresolved side bets but left resolved ones on the felt with their result, so a resumed session displayed a win it had already paid.
HandOutcome.INSURANCE_ONLY was declared, labelled and switch-cased, and never produced.

The session panel reported one net figure, so a hand that lost its wager and hit a side bet showed a positive total beside a hundred-percent loss rate. SeatStats now books sideNet and insuranceNet apart from the whole, and the panel breaks them out.

playRound read `handsBefore` after the deal and compared it against a value taken after settlement — but the deal is what increments handsPlayed, so the figure was always zero. It went unnoticed because nothing divided by it until the new per-thousand rule tests did. `insuranceWagered` had the same shape: read before the offers phase opened, so it was always zero too. Both are read at the right moment now, and strategy.test.ts checks the bot's own reporting against arithmetic over two thousand rounds.

The stats drawer covered the button that closes it. Below 1280px the rail is pinned right at z-40 and the header was not stacked at all, so on a narrow screen the drawer painted over the Stats button — found by driving the phone layout with a browser rather than by reading it.
defects2: The persist merge conjured money. A round is unwound on reload because it cannot be resumed honestly — but the driver parks a *finished* round at SETTLE for a couple of seconds so the figures can be read, and during that window `hand.bet` and `seat.insurance` are still populated even though settle() has already returned every stake. A reload there refunded them a second time: a $10 hand with $5 of winning insurance came back $15 up. The unwind now runs only when `!table.settled`, and it moved into the engine as `abandonRound` because it moves money and everything that moves money is testable engine code.

The house-edge model double-counted double-after-split. The 0.40% baseline is the published six-deck S17 *DAS* game, and DAS was then credited again — making every displayed figure 0.14 points too generous and printing a 0.09% player advantage on the Liberal Shoe preset, in a game whose premise is pricing rules honestly. The baseline is now a named constant describing the reference game, every rule is priced as a delta from it, and `estimateHouseEdge` is defined as that baseline less the sum of `ruleEffects` — so the breakdown in the setup screen cannot fail to add up to the headline beside it. Against the simulation the corrected model is now within 0.15 points on every preset and exact on single deck.

The card counter read the dealer's hole card. `countShoe` walked every card up to `shoe.pos`, and the hole card leaves the shoe at the top of the round — so the panel reported four cards seen on a hand with three face up, and the deviation bot knew what the dealer was holding. README, the HUD hint and the panel's own caption all claimed otherwise. `countTable` now excludes anything still face down, and every live-table reader goes through it.

A split-ace hand could be left live with no legal move. `stops()` decided at split time whether there was room under the hand limit, and a later split of a different hand could take the last slot — leaving earlier hands unable to hit (split aces never can) and unable to split, so standing was their only option and the focus stopped on them anyway. Room is now decided when the question is asked, by `sealSplitAces`.

The advisor could name an illegal move. Every fallback ended at HIT, which a split ace cannot do, so a `P` cell that could not be split recommended a play the dealer would refuse — and the trainer then marked the player's forced stand wrong. Every fallback checks the engine's legality map, and there is a test that no cell can produce an action the table would refuse.

`SeatStats.decisions` and `correctDecisions` were declared, documented and summed by the trainer panel, and incremented nowhere — the same family as the silently-zero findings before them. They are wired through `recordDecision`, and the panel shows a lifetime tally beside the rolling one.

The HUD's "measured edge" divided a numerator including side bets and insurance by a main-bet-only denominator — the exact mistake autoplay.ts warns about by name. It now measures the main game against the main wager, which is why sideNet and insuranceNet are broken out.
defects3: The shoe threw when it ran dry mid-round. `draw` raised on exhaustion, on the stated premise that the cut card made it unreachable — and three seats on the shipped Single Deck preset reached it in thirteen thousand rounds, because one deck cut at 65% leaves eighteen cards and three seats splitting to four hands can want more than that inside one hand. It threw out of a React event handler, in a codebase whose stated invariant is that actions return a refusal and never throw. It now does what a dealer does: `reshuffleKeeping` gathers the discards, leaves the cards on the felt where they are, shuffles and carries on. 200,000 rounds of three-seat single deck now run clean with zero duplicate cards in play.

The negative-edge guard covered five presets, not the space a player can build. One deck plus re-split aces plus hit split aces plus early surrender is four toggles from the setup screen and genuinely favours the player by about a percent — the model is right about that and the screen says so rather than clamping it. The test now sweeps all 2,880 reachable combinations, asserting the itemisation still sums to the headline everywhere and that the arithmetic stays in a sane band.

The stats drawer buried the action bar. Below 1280px the rail overlays, and on a phone in landscape it covered a third of the felt and the whole button row beneath it — the table was visible and Deal was not pressable. It now has a scrim that dismisses it on a tap anywhere else, scoped by the same media query as the rail so the tablet layout, where the rail is part of the page rather than over it, is not dimmed by a scrim with nothing to dismiss.

Bust It's tolerance was never justified. It was asserted at 0.3 points and passed two runs by luck; a change to the RNG stream (the shoe now draws a seed for its own next shuffle) shifted every seeded measurement and it failed at 0.41 — well inside the noise it has always had. The bet pays 400:1 on an eight-card dealer bust and that tail dominates: its per-round standard deviation is about 2.5 units against the main game's 1.15, so half a million rounds place it to within roughly a percent. The test now computes its own three-sigma band from the run, and the published figure is pooled over two million rounds: 6.92%, not 6.71%.
defects4: The edge model double-charged the soft-double restriction — the same mistake as the DAS double-count, in the same function, found by chasing down which preset kept drifting from its own measurement. A table that only doubles on 9-11 or 10-11 reads the restriction against the hand's total, and every soft total is thirteen or more, so it refuses every soft double already; the published cost of 'double 9-11 only' is quoted against a table that allowed soft doubling and therefore contains that loss. Charging both billed the player twice for one rule and made the European preset look 0.13 points worse than it is. With it fixed, every preset now sits within 0.093 points of the mean of two independent 800,000-round runs — European went from 0.22 out to the typical deviation. The setup screen also disables the soft-double toggle at a restricted table now, rather than offering a switch that does nothing.
defects5: The basic-strategy chart doubled soft eighteen against a two at S17, where the play is to stand. Doubling it is the H17 deviation, and SOFT_H17 carried an entry for that cell that changed nothing because the S17 chart already said the H17 answer — so the patch was dead and the S17 chart was wrong, at the default table, on the most common soft hand in the game. Forty chart assertions missed it because each asked about a cell rather than about the relationship between two charts; the new test asserts exactly which cells each rule moves, so a dead patch entry now fails whether or not its cell is asserted.

The store graded a decision, wrote it onto the seat, then made the engine call against a snapshot taken before the grade — so `apply` swapped the graded table back out. Every decision counted, every count discarded, and the HUD's session tally could never render. The store had no tests at all; it has six now, and they test the seam rather than the engine.

`setRules` was the one door into a wager that did not go through `setBet`, and walked past all of its checks. Raising the table minimum, which the setup dialog exposes, raised a standing bet without asking whether the seat could pay, and `deal` subtracted it: a $50 bankroll dealt a $100 hand ended at minus fifty. `setRules` now ends with `setBet`'s invariants and `deal` refuses rather than paying out money that is not there.

The dealer distribution was asserted against remembered round numbers, two of which were wrong — 17.58% for a twenty against a true 17.953%, and 28.32% for the bust rate against 28.192% — behind tolerances of six and eight sigma while the comment beside them claimed three, and named a sample size the test does not use. The README then reported a correct dealer as low against a figure that was itself the error. The reference is computed exactly now, the recursion is written out at the foot of the file, and the bands are derived from the figure and the sample size.

The measured house edge was per unit of action while the model beside it is per initial wager. Basic strategy puts about 1.133 units on the felt per unit bet, so the two differ by roughly 12% in relative terms — under the noise floor, which is why it survived five rounds of review comparing a measurement to a model it was not a measurement of.

Even money was offered wherever the payout was not 1:1, but the engine books it only at 3:2 — no insurance stake guarantees one unit at 6:5. The shipped Single Deck preset is 6:5, so the button was live and answered with a refusal.

Accessibility: no focus style existed anywhere (the user agent's ring, on a dark green felt), the modal never moved, trapped or restored focus, and the game's shortcuts stayed live underneath an open dialog — so pressing D while reading the strategy chart doubled the hand behind it.

Persistence serialised and wrote the whole ~150 KB slice synchronously on every state change, fifteen to twenty times a round. Writes are coalesced and held until the felt is at rest — rehydration abandons an in-flight round anyway, so those writes were of state no reload could use — and forced on pagehide. One write per round.

`splitAcesBlackjack` was a rule field the types said the engine consults and nothing read; removed, with the reason left where a reader would look for it. The autoplay bot on the felt insured against a dealer ten whenever early surrender had opened the offers phase, and never took early surrender at all while the simulation's bot always has — so the two bots disagreed about a rule the setup screen prices at 0.63%.
defects6: The counting trainer offered four systems and was calibrated for one. `edgeAt`, `betRamp`, `deviationFor` and `insuranceIsGood` are all indexed in Hi-Lo true counts and were handed whatever the selected system produced — so Knock-Out, whose running count starts at -4*(decks-1), reported a 10.4% player disadvantage on an untouched six-deck shoe and fired every at-or-below index play permanently. There is now a `hiLo` field on the count that every consumer reads, and a test that asserts a shoe nobody has dealt from is neutral in all four systems and produces no index play through the bot.

The round-five denominator fix reached the simulation and not the stats panel, which is where a player actually reads the number: it divided by total action and printed 0.298% two rows under a model saying 0.40%. `SeatStats` gained `staked`, which moves only at the deal, and the persist version was bumped to 3 with a migration — plus the test that proves the migration, since round four's lesson was a required field added without one.

The global keyboard handler exempted only form fields, so Enter and Space — the two keys every button is activated with — were swallowed and preventDefault-ed before the focused control saw them. Focusing Paytables and pressing Enter dealt a round; focusing Stats during a hand and pressing Space stood the hand. The whole header was keyboard-inoperable.

Side-bet house edges were the six-deck figures, printed with no qualifier on the felt chip, in the rules editor and in the paytable dialog — inches from the deck selector. Perfect Pairs needs a second copy of an identical card, so at one deck it is impossible and costs 47.06%, not the 6.11% shown. The enumeration moved from the test file into `sidebets.ts` and every one of those three places now prices the shoe in front of the player. Bust It has no closed form and is marked as measured at six decks rather than silently repriced.

Disabled action buttons carried their refusal in `title=` under `disabled:pointer-events-none` — a tooltip that can never fire, for anyone. The reasons are printed under the action bar now, with `aria-describedby` linking each button to its own.

The advisor could still name an action the buttons reject, which is the invariant its own comment states. During the offers phase at an early-surrender table the engine allows exactly one action, and every fallback ended at STAND — so the hint bar named STAND and the trainer graded a correct early surrender as a mistake. The fallback is now whatever the table will actually book, asserted over all 31 non-empty legality maps against all ten chart codes.

Early surrender was priced at 0.63% and advised off the late-surrender chart, which is the same chart. The hard-total cells of the standard early-surrender set are now applied when the rule is EARLY. The pair cells of that set are deliberately not — see openItems.

`rebet` checked the bankroll and the maximum and not the minimum, so a table minimum raised between rounds let last round's smaller wager back into the circle. A store test that only passed in file order. A test named 'splits on soft seventeen' that asserts the dealer draws. And the focus ring's black halo was a box-shadow inside `:where()`, so every button carrying a Tailwind shadow utility overrode it.
defects7: `sideBetEdgeIsExact` returned true for Lucky Ladies while the enumeration's own comment called its jackpot term an approximation — so the paytable dialog printed 'enumerated exactly' over a figure that was not. It is exact now: the enumeration already knows which two cards the player holds, so the dealer's natural rate conditioned on them is a closed form, and the flat rate it used before was wrong in the direction that flattered the bet.

Two of the eight round-six fixes shipped with no test: `rebet`'s minimum-bet gate and the Enter/Space keyboard guard. Deleting either left the suite green. `rebet` — the third door into a betting circle — had no test at all after five rounds of review, and now has four. The keyboard decision is a pure exported function over (key, element) with its own test file, because the logic that two consecutive rounds got wrong from opposite sides was living inside a DOM event handler in a suite that runs in node.

The round-six keyboard fix traded a header bug for a felt bug: it yielded Enter and Space to any focused button, and a mouse click leaves focus on the button it clicked — so after clicking Hit, Space re-hit the hand instead of standing it, which is the shortcut the README leads with. `:focus-visible` is the distinction the platform already draws and exactly the one wanted: a keyboard user's Enter reaches their button, a mouse user's Space still stands the hand.

`stats.blackjacks` was incremented only by the BLACKJACK outcome, so a player natural against a dealer natural — which pushes — was never counted, under a caption reading 'naturals dealt'. Over three million rounds that reads 4.55% against a true 4.749%, and the missing 4.2% is exactly the dealer-natural rate. Same shape as the wagered-versus-staked mix-up.

`sideBetEdge` ran a 140,608-term enumeration synchronously inside render — once per seat per enabled bet on the felt, and for all six kinds on every keystroke in the rules editor. Stepping the deck selector from eight to one paid about sixty milliseconds five times over, inside React. The eight-by-five table is a constant now and the enumeration is the thing that proves it: a test recomputes every cell.

Two tests did not constrain what their names claimed. The Hi-Lo conversion test restated the implementation (`12/3/2 === 2`) and would have passed for any scale factor; it now measures the conversion against the actual Hi-Lo count of fifteen hundred shoe states, which is how the Knock-Out residual below came to be known at all. The early-surrender test asserted 'the charts differ only against a ten and an ace', which does not say which cells moved — a chart surrendering hard 8 against an ace would have passed. It now pins the exact nine-cell delta.

Three pieces of copy described pre-round-six behaviour: the Measured edge tooltip said 'a fraction of what you wagered' while the code divides by what was staked, the paytable dialog hard-coded '6.11% at six decks' into a paragraph whose own comment argues nothing should be written into the prose, and the equity chart's label read 'Session result' for what is a 160-round window sitting four rows under a whole-session Net figure.

Side-bet prices reached a mouse and nothing else: the chip's aria-label named the bet and its wager but not its house edge, which is the one number the game exists to attach — and worth least to the player who cannot hover. The persist comment claimed a migrate case for version 2 that does not exist (it is handled at the point of use instead), and the refusal line was hidden while the driver was busy, leaving the buttons' aria-describedby dangling.
defects8: The early-surrender cells added the round before were applied first and then overwritten by `FEW_DECK_ONE` and `ENHC`, both written for a chart with no surrender in it. At ENHC the chart surrendered hard sixteen against an ace while *hitting* eight-eight against an ace — the same hand — and surrendered the weaker seven-seven beside it; at one deck it surrendered hard fourteen against a ten while standing on seven-seven. Exactly the trap the pair cells were added to close, reopened one line later. Early surrender is applied last now, which is also right on the merits: every overridden cell is a rule about committing a second chip, and surrender commits none. Every early-surrender test had been pinned to `defaultRules()`, which is why 181 green tests could not see it; the new one sweeps deck count, hole-card rule and soft-17 rule.

The autoplay bet ramp, the Illustrious 18 deviations and the even-money branch were all gated on a bot config that `setBot` could set and nothing in the app called — so the counting panel showed a ramp beside a bot that flat-bet, and three code paths fixed the round before were unreachable. The two switches are in the counting panel now. A betting ramp displayed next to a bot that ignores it is the same defect as a rule switch priced at 0.08% that does nothing, and this project has now shipped that shape three times.

Autoplay's first bet-placement fix swept the player's own chips away: it reset every occupied seat's wager to the bot's unit whenever autoplay was on, and `setBet` caps a side bet to the main wager, so a $100 bet with $50 on Lucky Ladies became $10 and $10, silently, on a 300ms timer. It is gated on the spread switch now — a flat bot has no opinion about bet size — and clamped against what the side bets leave in the bankroll.

The pointer-only sweep, in its fifth round: `Stat` carried five substantive explanations in a `title` on a bare div, which reaches a mouse and nothing else — they are repeated to assistive technology now. The dealing-speed and new-session buttons are emoji-only and take their accessible name from the emoji rather than the `title`, so they have `aria-label`s. The strategy chart rendered `Rs` and `Rp` while its legend named neither.

`rebuy` had been in the engine, tested, since the first draft with no UI — so a seat busted below the table minimum could only be recovered with New session, which wipes every bankroll and the whole statistics panel. There is a Rebuy button now. `playForMe` was dead in the same way while `autoplay.ts` claimed the app used it for a 'play it for me' button; that button exists now too.

Five claims that no longer matched the code, one un-guarded preset button that answered mid-round with a refusal toast beside a neighbour that disables itself and says why, and dialog shortcuts that could not switch from one dialog to another.

stack.state: zustand 5 + persist; immer 11 on the engine's cold paths only — see keyDecisions
stack.motion: CSS keyframes and transitions; motion 13 is a dependency but the table does not currently need it
stack.art: ../../cardArt copied into public/cards at build time by being committed there

commands.test: pnpm test — 183 tests, about two seconds. Run this constantly.
commands.testStats: pnpm run test:stats — 29 tests, about seven and a half minutes. Dealer distributions, five presets, six rule wiring checks, six side bets, counting. Opt-in, separate config.
commands.lint: pnpm run lint — zero errors and zero warnings; keep it that way, it caught the two selector loops' cousins before they shipped.
commands.note: All commands run from TableGames/blackjack. The repository root has no build.
commands.start: pnpm start — serves the built out/ statically on :3002. NOT `next start`, which a static export does not have.

architecture.principle: The engine is pure. src/lib/engine and src/lib/strategy contain no React, no I/O, no clock, and no randomness at the point of use — the two functions that need it (deal, and the constructors) take an Rng as an argument. Every action returns a new table or a refusal. That is what makes a session replayable from a seed, testable without a browser, and safe to drive from a bot and a simulation at the same time.
architecture.storeIsAMetronome: src/lib/store/useGame.ts owns the pacing of a round — the gaps between cards, the pause before the hole card, how long a settlement sits on the felt — and nothing else. Every money-moving call delegates to an engine function and swaps in whatever table comes back, so the store cannot invent a payout. Everything the driver does, a player could do by hand.
architecture.oneRulebook: The bot calls hit(), stand(), double(), split() and surrender() — the same exported functions the buttons call. There is no second path into the state, which is why a bot cannot make a bet a player could not, and why the simulation measures the game the felt actually plays.
architecture.svgPlusDom: The felt is an SVG at a fixed viewBox; the cards, chips and totals are HTML positioned in the same coordinate space and scaled by one transform on a wrapper. SVG draws the screen-printed lettering far better and CSS animates a card flip far better, and this is the seam that lets each do what it is good at while sharing one set of coordinates. Surface.tsx measures the container and passes the scale down, because a card at 62px is right and at 20px is illegible — the card size is a function of the scale, not a constant.

keyDecisions: Money is integer cents. A 3:2 blackjack on a five dollar bet pays seven fifty, so dollars have to be fractional somewhere; cents put the fraction in the integer. Payouts floor, never round up — a dealer short-pays to the nearest chip. Over the millions of rounds the simulation deals, float dollars would accumulate an error the same size as the thing being measured.
The shoe is an array plus a pointer, not a shifted queue. Immutability plus shift() means copying the tail of a 416-card array per card dealt.

immer was removed from every hot path. It remains on the cold ones — placing a bet, sitting down, changing the rules — where it runs at most once a round and its readability is free. The reason is measured, not stylistic: immer's cost is proportional to what a recipe READS, and drafting a seat drafts its hands, drafting a hand drafts its card array, and reading a card drafts the card. A round of blackjack reads all of that. See the note above updateSeat in table.ts.

Assigning a shoe INSIDE an immer draft was 84% of the simulation's runtime on its own: immer's finaliser walks any new plain value looking for nested drafts, which meant walking four hundred card objects for a field whose only change was an integer. Every draw is now hoisted out of the draft and the shoe is spread back on by withShoe(). Do not put a shoe in a draft.
settle() attaches the round history with a plain spread rather than inside a produce, for the same reason: prepending to a three-hundred-entry list inside a draft made immer rescan every record.
Together those three changes took a simulated round from 1,581 microseconds to 24 — sixty-six times. Nothing about the game changed; 114 tests passed before and after each step.

The strategy chart has the table's own restrictions folded into its cells, not just into the advisor. A cell reading 'surrender' at a table with no surrender is a play the dealer will refuse, printed under a caption claiming otherwise. adviseFrom() still has the fallback logic and is still tested, because it is the honest description of what a printed card means.

Side-bet edges are computed, not cited. Five of the six are decided by two or three cards off the top, so sidebets.sim.test.ts enumerates every ordered pair and triple weighted by exact probability. Where a remembered figure and the enumeration disagreed, the enumeration won — Perfect Pairs at six decks is 6.11%, not the widely quoted 4.10% (that is the eight-deck number for this paytable, and the bet genuinely improves with more decks because a perfect pair needs a second copy of the identical card).

The Bust It ladder was repriced. The first draft measured at 20.3%, which is worse than Lucky Ladies and not a bet any house spreads; 1/3/8/20/75/400 measures at 6.71% and has the escalating shape a real one has.

Insurance and even money are one code path. Even money is insurance for the maximum on a natural and comes to exactly 1:1 on the main wager either way the hole card falls; implementing it separately is how the two end up disagreeing. There is a test that asserts the payout is identical for both hole cards.

ENHC is a separate settlement path, not a cosmetic flag. Under no-hole-card the dealer's second card arrives after the doubling is done, so a natural takes the doubled and split chips as well. That is the whole 0.11% and there is a test for exactly that hand.

The counting trainer reads the discard tray and nothing else. countShoe walks cards[0..pos) — the cards a player has seen. composition() could answer far more accurately and is deliberately wired to nothing but the tests.

The dealer plays out their hand when a Bust It bet is live even if every player hand has busted, because Bust It is a bet on the dealer's finished hand. dealerMustPlay() is the predicate and it is asked once per turn, not once per card.

Chart cell colours and side-bet accents live in a plain :root block, not in @theme. Tailwind 4 only emits a theme variable when a utility referencing it is generated, and these are only ever read through var() in an inline style because the value is chosen at runtime — declared in @theme they were tree-shaken out and every chart cell rendered with no background.

The felt's three printed arcs are concentric, struck from one centre below the table. Two arcs with independently chosen radii and chords cross, which is exactly what the first version did — the payout line and the dealer's rule overlapped in the middle of the table.

Side-bet circles are one row of six compact boxes. Two rows do not fit: the felt's arc closes in fast below the betting circles and an outside seat's second row hangs over the rail. This is the constraint that sets the seat spacing.
No service worker, no analytics, no network calls at runtime. The fonts are self-hosted by the build and the card art is served from the same origin.

Even money is offered only at 3:2, and that is arithmetic rather than convention. Insuring a natural for x returns 2x on a dealer natural and p - x otherwise; guaranteeing 1 needs x = 1/2 from the first and x = p - 1 from the second, and those agree only at p = 3/2. At 6:5 no stake makes the offer even money, so the table does not make it and says why. Insurance stays available, because it is a different bet.

A side bet's contingent winnings are recorded on the wager, not recomputed at settlement. Lucky Ladies' top line needs the dealer's hand, which is unknown when the bet is graded; recomputing it later reads a hand a split may have taken apart. SideBetWager.jackpot holds the amount from grade time.

The rule tests assert frequencies, not edge deltas. Blackjack's per-hand standard deviation is about 1.15 units, so a difference between two 300,000-round arms carries a three-sigma band of 0.89% — wider than DAS (0.14%), late surrender (0.08%), ENHC (0.11%) or H17 (0.22%) combined. Resolving 0.14% would take fifty million rounds an arm. So those rows are printed as diagnostics and what is asserted is how often the bot doubles, splits or surrenders, which is near-binomial and converges in seconds. That is also the only test shape that catches a rule wired to nothing.

The counting claim is asserted where it converges. Spread-versus-flat is a coin flip at this length because a 1-12 spread's variance is several times a flat bet's; instead a flat bettor's result is bucketed by the true count at the deal, and the rich bucket must beat the poor one by a point. Same evidence that the shoe is real, an order of magnitude tighter.

The edge model is defined by a named reference game rather than a bare baseline constant, and `estimateHouseEdge` is that game's edge less the sum of `ruleEffects`. Deriving the number and its itemisation from one list is what makes them agree; when they were computed separately, the panel credited '+0.22 dealer stands on all 17s' against a baseline that already stood on all seventeens, and double-counted DAS on top. A rule the reference game already has is priced as a penalty when absent, never a bonus when present.

The counting trainer takes what is *visible*, not what has left the shoe. Those differ by exactly one card — the dealer's hole card — and that difference is the whole distinction between a trainer and a cheat. `countTable` is the only function anything should call during a round.

The Super Sevens bonus card is drawn on the felt rather than discarded. It was simpler to consume it silently, but a card that leaves the shoe unseen is a card the counter would be counting behind the player's back — so it is stored on the wager and shown.

The felt has two geometries, not one scale factor. A blackjack table needs about 520 units of depth for the dealer's cards, three printed lines, the players' cards, the circles, the side-bet spots and a nameplate — and a phone in landscape has roughly 290 pixels of height once the header and button bar have taken theirs, so scaling that shape left two thirds of an 844-pixel screen black. The shallow geometry drops to one printed line and moves the nameplate into the header's territory, buying back 150 units of depth; it also pulls the outside seats inward, because the shallow arc closes on the rail much faster and six side-bet spots under an outside seat would hang over it. Both are described by the same `FeltGeometry` fields, so nothing downstream branches: Surface measures the container, `geometryFor` picks one, and every coordinate follows. Phone landscape went from 61% of the width to 84%.

The shoe carries the seed of its own next shuffle. A shoe that runs out mid-round has to reshuffle, and that needs randomness — but threading a generator through every function that deals a card would have changed five signatures and every test that calls them, to serve a case that fires once in thirteen thousand rounds. `ShoeState.seed` keeps the reshuffle deterministic and replayable while leaving `hit`, `double`, `split` and `dealerStep` pure functions of the table.

A tolerance that only holds on the seeds you happened to try is not a test. Where a measurement's band cannot be argued for from first principles, the test computes it from the run — Bust It does this — and where no feasible sample size can resolve the effect at all, the row is printed as a diagnostic and something else is asserted instead.

A rule's published cost is quoted against a specific baseline, and the model has to know which. Double-after-split was credited on top of a baseline that already had it; soft doubling was charged on top of a restriction that already forbade it. Both looked like separate switches and were the same rule counted twice. Before adding a term, ask what the figure is a delta *from* — and prefer a check that the engine agrees the rule bites at all, which is what `agrees with the engine about which doubles are legal` does.
gotchas: deal() takes an Rng because a reshuffle happens there. It is the only action that does.

A hand's `bet` already includes any double, and the stake has already left the bankroll. settleHand returns both `net` (the signed change, what the ledger reads) and `returned` (what goes back to the bankroll). Conflating them is how a settlement function pays doubles twice; they are named apart everywhere.
isBlackjack() takes splitDepth. Ace-ten on a split hand is twenty-one and pays even money at every casino on earth. Getting it wrong is worth about a tenth of a percent.
advance()/settleFocus() must NOT pass the turn after a hit that leaves the hand live, or after a split. Most moves do not end the turn. This was a real bug.

The INSURANCE phase carries two offers, not one: insurance against an ace, and early surrender against a ten or an ace. It is entered for either, and closeOffers() is what triggers the peek. An early surrender that finishes the last hand must not skip that.
settle() is guarded by table.settled. The UI drives it off a phase transition and a transition can fire twice.

The store's persist merge() force-settles a round that was in flight when the tab closed: chips on hands and unresolved side bets go back to the bankroll and the phase resets to BETTING. There is no honest way to resume a half-committed round whose timers are gone.
lastBets is a Map and is deliberately not persisted — JSON has no Maps, and it would come back as {} and silently break the re-bet button.
Never use advice() or count() as zustand selectors. They build a fresh object per call. Use useAdvice() and useCount().

The simulation tops the bankroll back up rather than letting the bot go broke. A run that stops at round 40,000 has measured 40,000 rounds and then stopped, which biases the sample toward losing runs.

Distribution measurements need a live Bust It bet, otherwise about three rounds in a hundred end with the dealer standing pat on a two-card twelve and the numbers are not comparable to a published table.

The paired rule-delta tests share a seed but not a card sequence: a rule change alters how many cards come off the shoe and the two runs diverge within a few rounds. They check a sign and an order of magnitude. The absolute figures are in the preset tests.
public/cards is a committed copy of ../../cardArt. A static export cannot reach outside its own public directory. If the shared deck changes, copy it again.
next dev writes AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md into the project root unless agentRules is disabled. They are gitignored.

Split aces stay live when they draw another ace and the table re-splits them. `canHit` still refuses, so the only legal moves are SPLIT and STAND. Marking them done unconditionally is what made resplitAces a no-op for the whole first draft.
chartFor's cache key must include every rule the chart reads. It omitted holeCard and served a peeking chart to a no-hole-card table.

Chart cell colours and side-bet accents must stay in a plain :root block. Tailwind 4 only emits an @theme variable when a utility referencing it is generated, and these are read through var() in inline styles.

Rules in globals.css that target the same single class as a Tailwind utility win, because they come after it in the cascade. The .stats-rail block is scoped :not(.hidden) for exactly this reason — without it, opening the tall-viewport layout overrode the `hidden` utility and showed a panel the player had closed.
A `role="status"` element has to exist before text lands in it. Rendering the toast stack only when there is a toast means the first message of a session is never announced.

playRound's before-and-after readings are order-sensitive: handsPlayed is incremented by deal() and insurance is placed after it, so one must be read before the deal and the other after the offers close. Both were wrong in the same way and both were silently zero.
Never call `countShoe` on a live table; call `countTable`. The difference is the dealer's hole card, and getting it wrong makes the trainer read cards the player cannot see.
A finished round sits at phase SETTLE for the settlement hold with its stakes already returned but still displayed. Anything that refunds 'what is at risk' has to check `table.settled` first.

Whether a split ace may be split again depends on how many hands the seat holds *now*, not how many it held when that hand was created. Deciding it at split time orphans hands that a later split makes unsplittable.

A mid-round reshuffle leaves the shoe smaller than decks x 52, because the cards on the felt are excluded from it. `isCompleteShoe` is therefore only meaningful on a shoe that was built between rounds.

`canDouble` reads a total restriction against the hand's *total*, soft or hard — so a 9-11 table refuses every soft double, and `doubleSoft` is inert there. The pricing model and the setup screen both depend on that; if it ever changes, all three have to change together.

automated: 183 unit tests covering hand mathematics, the peek, splits to four hands, split and re-split aces, doubling restrictions, both surrender rules, insurance and even money, ENHC, all six side bets, betting limits, the round lifecycle, abandoning a round, the whole strategy chart cell by cell, the advisor's legality, the four counting systems, and — since round five — the store itself: that a graded decision reaches the seat, that a refusal becomes a toast rather than a state change, that no rules change leaves a wager the bankroll cannot cover, and that a round is one write to storage rather than twenty; and — since round seven — that re-betting respects every limit `setBet` does, that the precomputed side-bet edge table matches the enumeration at every deck count from one to eight, and that the keyboard yields a keystroke to a focused control only when the keyboard put focus there.

Bankroll conservation across a split with two doubles: whatever the round did, the bankroll at the end equals the bankroll at the start plus the sum of the signed results. It is the one assertion that catches a stake taken and not returned, or returned twice, anywhere in the money path.

Dealer finishing distribution asserted against an exact recursion over the six-deck composition — not against published round numbers — with each tolerance computed as three binomial standard errors at the sample size in use: 0.163 on the finishing totals, 0.191 on the bust rate, 0.090 on naturals. The 0.5 and 0.4 this line used to advertise were six and eight sigma, and were how a wrong reference table went four rounds without failing.
Player natural frequency asserted against the exact 4.749% within its own three-sigma band (0.090 points at 500,000 rounds).
Five rule sets' house edges asserted within three standard errors of the rule model.

The edge model swept across all 25,920 tables the setup screen can build — every combination of the eleven live controls — asserting that the itemisation sums to the headline and that the extremes stay where they should: about one percent to the player at the most generous, about three and a half to the house at a carnival table paying even money on a natural.

Six side-bet edges: five enumerated exactly and asserted to 0.06 points, one measured against a band the test computes for itself. The enumeration also runs at every deck count from one to eight and is asserted against the precomputed table the felt reads, so the number printed on a chip is derived from the paytable rather than remembered.
Shoe completeness asserted after every reshuffle across twenty thousand rounds.
A counted 1-12 spread asserted to beat a flat bet on the same shoes — which is the evidence that the shoe is a real shoe and the discard tray really reflects it.
manual: Played in a real browser at 1440x860: three seats, all six side bets, insurance, the chart dialog, the paytable dialog, the rules editor, the counting panel and the trainer. Zero console errors.

prefers-reduced-motion verified in a real browser with the setting on: every animation resolves to `none` and every transition to 0s, and a dealt hand renders correctly with the hole card down rather than stuck mid-flip.

Keyboard-only play verified: space deals, S stands, and the round runs to settlement without a pointer. The focus ring this line used to claim did not exist — the app defined no focus style at all and inherited the user agent's, which is a thin dark outline on a dark green felt. There is a brass :focus-visible ring now, the dialogs trap and restore focus, and the game's own shortcuts stand down while one is open. The ring and the trap have been read in the code and exercised in a browser; a full keyboard pass over every dialog has not been redone since.
Checked at 844x390 (iPhone landscape). The felt is height-constrained there — see openItems.
notVerified: Sound has not been listened to. Every voice is synthesised and the levels were chosen by analogy with the craps mixer rather than measured; that file's own header says to measure rather than nudge, and nobody has.
Touch interaction on a real phone. The layout was checked at phone dimensions in a desktop browser, which is not the same thing.
The PWA install path (Share -> Add to Home Screen) has not been run on an actual iPhone.
Docker build and the nginx config are adapted from craps with the paths, ports and a card-art cache rule changed, and have not been built here.
Screen readers. The controls carry roles and labels and the felt's decorative SVG is aria-hidden, but nothing has been driven with VoiceOver or NVDA.

lastRun.note: What the suite printed on its last full run (29 tests, about 7m35s), against the corrected model and the corrected denominator. Re-run unchanged after round six: the counting rework is the identity for Hi-Lo, which is what the measuring bot counts in, and no preset ships early surrender — so every row reproduced to the digit, which is the cheapest evidence there is that the rework changed only what it meant to. Kept so a future change is compared against real numbers rather than against the tolerances that admit them.

sideBetEdges.BustIt: 6.92, measured rather than enumerated; the test computes its own three-sigma band per run

lastRun.counting: A flat bettor's own hands, bucketed by the true count as the round was dealt: +1.450% for the player at a true count of +2 or better against -2.804% at -2 or worse. That gap is the assertion.
lastRun.resplitAces: +0.060% against a model of +0.080%. Before the fix it was worth exactly nothing, because it did nothing.
lastRun.watchThis: RESOLVED. European measuring 0.347 points from the model was not noise — it was the soft-double restriction being charged on top of a double restriction that already forbids it. Left here as the record of what a preset drifting from its own measurement turned out to mean the one time it was chased down rather than filed.
lastRun.caveat: The six per-rule delta rows are printed diagnostics, not assertions, and cannot be otherwise: a difference between two 300,000-round arms carries a three-sigma band of 0.89%, wider than DAS, late surrender, ENHC and H17 combined. What is asserted for each rule is a frequency — doubles, splits and surrenders per thousand hands — which converges in seconds and is the only shape that catches a rule wired to nothing.
lastRun.modelAccuracy: Every preset is inside 0.24 points and inside its own three-sigma band. Vegas Strip is now the loosest at 0.237 against a 0.387 tolerance, and Single Deck the tightest at 0.033; correcting the denominator tightened three presets and loosened one, which is what a denominator change should look like rather than a uniform shift. The mean absolute gap across the five is 0.10 points.
lastRun.denominator: Every edge above is per unit of the initial wager, which is what the model and the published figures mean. Until round five the suite divided by the total action instead — about 1.133 units per unit bet under basic strategy — which reported every figure roughly 12% low in relative terms while comparing it to a model quoted the other way.
lastRun.exactReferences: The dealer rows are asserted against an exact recursion over the six-deck composition, not against published round numbers: S17 bust 28.192%, H17 bust 28.576%, and 17/18/19/20/21 at 14.525/13.926/13.368/17.953/12.036. The table that used to be here had the twenty wrong by 0.37 points and the bust rate by 0.19, behind tolerances of six and eight sigma described in the comment as three.
lastRun.vegasStripPooled: Round seven's standing question, settled: the Vegas Strip preset's 0.637% against a model of 0.400% is noise, not a model error and not a chart imperfection. Pooled over three million rounds across three seeds it is 0.408% +/- 0.066 (1 sigma) — an eighth of a standard error from the model. The single-seed spread (0.549 / 0.341 / 0.335) is exactly the 1.15/sqrt(N) the per-hand standard deviation predicts. Supporting evidence gathered at the same time: win/lose/push renormalised to settled hands is 43.57/47.88/8.54 against a published 43.3/48.0/8.7, and the action-to-stake ratio is 1.1317 against the documented 1.133.

openItems: Early surrender implements the standard Atlantic City 1978 set in full: hard 5-7 and 12-17 against an ace, hard 14-16 against a ten, and the four pairs whose hard total is already in that list (3,3 / 6,6 / 7,7 / 8,8 against an ace; 7,7 / 8,8 against a ten). The pair cells are separate lines only because a pair is looked up in the pair chart and never reaches the hard entry that plainly applies to it — which is exactly why they went missing when the hard cells went in. Adding them also settled an inconsistency: PAIRS_H17 surrenders 8,8 against an ace, so an early-surrender table used to advise that hand differently depending on the dealer's soft-17 rule, which has nothing to do with when the peek happens.
Side-bet strategy is not advised at all. Several of these bets have count-dependent plays; the trainer says nothing about them.

The rule model agrees with the simulation on every preset, and the presets are measured one seed at a time. A single 800,000-round run places an edge to about +/- 0.13, which is wider than most of the rule effects the model prices — so a preset row drifting by two tenths is not evidence of anything until it is pooled. Vegas Strip was chased down exactly that way in round seven and came back as noise. What would make this properly tight is pooling several seeds per preset in the suite, which costs a few million rounds a run and has not been done.

The shallow felt drops the insurance line and the dealer's rule from the print, because there is no depth for them. Both are still in the HUD and the help dialog, but a player on a phone reads them off a panel rather than off the felt.
No multi-hand-per-seat betting (two boxes at one seat), which some tables allow.
The equity chart caps at 300 rounds of history and has no zoom.

The dialogs have keyboard shortcuts now (C chart, B side bets, comma setup, ? help, Escape to close), and once open one traps focus, restores it on close and stands the game's own shortcuts down. What has still not been done is a full keyboard pass over every control inside every dialog.
Docker image size is unmeasured. The card deck adds about 2 MB over the craps image.

The dialog focus trap and the :focus-visible ring were added in round five and read in a browser, but no screen reader has been driven over them. The `notVerified` note about VoiceOver and NVDA still stands.

The app's autoplay bot and the simulation's bot are two implementations of the same policy in two files. They agree on early surrender, on when insurance is offered, on the betting ramp and on even money — and the counting panel now has the two switches (ramp, index plays) that make the app's half of that reachable at all; before round eight `setBot` had no caller, so the app's bot was permanently flat and chart-only and three of those agreements were between one live implementation and one dead one. Nothing enforces that the two stay in step.

The Hi-Lo equivalence is now measured against the shoe rather than argued for: over fifteen hundred shoe states at 1, 2, 6 and 8 decks it is unbiased for Omega II and Hi-Opt II (inside sampling error) and runs about 0.09 true counts low for Knock-Out. That residual is real and has a cause — the derivation inverts an unconditional expectation of sevens seen, while the quantity wanted is conditional on the count in hand — and no single linear map removes it. It is worth about 0.05% of edge against integer index numbers, so it changes no decision the game makes. What is still not done is a check against published per-system index tables, which would be the right way to settle the level-two conversion rather than the shoe-based one used here.

Side-bet edges are enumerated for the table's own deck count, but only for a fresh shoe. A player who bets Perfect Pairs deep into a depleted shoe faces a different number, and nothing anywhere says so — the count panel is the only part of the game that knows the shoe has been dealt from.

Late surrender is priced at 0.08% and early surrender at 0.63%, and `chartFor` gives the late chart to a LATE table — but under ENHC the dealer has no hole card when the decision is made, so a late surrender buys out of the dealer's natural exactly as an early one does. At a LATE+ENHC table the two rules are close to the same bet, and the model charges eight times more for one of them and advises the weaker chart. No preset ships that combination; the setup screen can build it.

`Stat`'s explanatory tooltips are now repeated to assistive technology as visually-hidden text, so they reach a screen reader as well as a mouse — but a touch user still cannot get at them, because there is no hover on a phone and these are read-only rows with no tap target. Printing them would need the stats panel redesigned around longer rows.

repoNotes.git: The repository is rooted at KnotzCrapzNCardz and published at https://github.com/KnotEnvy/KnotzCrapzNCardz (public).
repoNotes.structure: Games are self-contained apps under their own folders. TableGames/blackjack carries its own package.json, .gitignore and README; the root carries a repo-wide .gitignore and an index README. There is no root build.
repoNotes.ports: craps 8080, Dragon's Shrine 8081, blackjack 8082 — so all three run at once from the root compose file.
repoNotes.sharedAssets: ../../cardArt is the source of the 54-card deck. It is copied, not referenced: a static export cannot reach outside public/.

thenRead: src/lib/engine/table.ts — the state machine, and the note above updateSeat explaining why half of it is immer and half is not.
src/lib/engine/sidebets.sim.test.ts — the enumeration. It is the most unusual thing in here and the pattern generalises.
safestPlacesToStart: Adding a side bet: write the paytable in sidebets.ts, a resolver, a case in gradeSideBet, and an enumeration in the sim test. The test will tell you the edge; publish that number.
Adding a rule preset: rules.ts only. The setup screen, the shorthand and the chart all read from it.
Visual work on the felt: Felt.tsx is geometry and print, Surface.tsx is everything that moves. Neither can change what the game costs.
Sound: audio.ts is self-contained and every voice is independent.
riskiestPlacesToChange: resolve.ts settleHand — the five branches are in precedence order and the order is the rules.
table.ts settleFocus/openPlayerPhase — turn order is where the subtle bugs were, and three of the six found this session were here.
Anything that puts the shoe back inside an immer draft. It will not fail a test; it will quietly make the simulation twenty times slower.
basic.ts chart cells — a wrong cell moves the measured edge by less than the simulation's noise floor, so the unit tests are the only thing guarding them. Add a test with the cell.

deployment.model: Static. The game is client-side end to end, so next build runs with output: 'export' and writes out/ — a folder of files. No Node runs in production.
deployment.consequence: Anything requiring a server — route handlers, server actions, ISR, next/image optimisation — now fails the build instead of silently not working. That is the intended trade.
deployment.image: Two-stage Dockerfile: node:24-alpine builds, nginx:1.29-alpine serves. Runs read_only with tmpfs for nginx scratch dirs.
deployment.buildNeedsNetwork: next/font/google fetches Inter and Oswald during the build and self-hosts them into out/. An offline build machine fails at pnpm run build.
deployment.cardArt: public/cards is served with a one-year immutable cache. It never changes and a re-deal must not go back to the network for a card the browser already has.
deployment.tls: nginx.conf is an origin server speaking plain HTTP on 80. TLS belongs at a reverse proxy or tunnel in front of it.
deployment.docs: DEPLOY.md — the container, LAN play on a phone, and the options for public hosting.

pwa.what: public/manifest.webmanifest plus icons in public/icons. Installs to an iPhone home screen via Share → Add to Home Screen, opening standalone.
pwa.orientation: Landscape. Portrait under 560px tall shows a 'turn your phone sideways' overlay rather than a squeezed table.
pwa.appleTags: Next 16 emits only the standardised mobile-web-app-capable. The legacy apple-mobile-web-app-capable is added by hand via metadata.other, because iPhones a couple of versions back read only that spelling.
pwa.manifestMime: nginx does not know .webmanifest natively. The types block in nginx.conf sets application/manifest+json — without it iOS silently refuses the install.
pwa.notDone: No service worker, so the installed app still needs the network to load.
